implementation_notes: Node ships assertion functions in the standard library: assert.ok, assert.strictEqual, assert.fail and friends throw assert.AssertionError on failure, and importing strict mode makes the non-strict comparators behave strictly. This is the default realization for server-side JavaScript, where no assert statement exists; the module is always on, so it plays the role of an always-checked guard rather than a debug-only assertion.
pitfalls: console.assert only logs and never throws, so it is not an assertion mechanism; a broken invariant can pass unnoticed in production while the console fills up.
AssertionError can be swallowed by a broad catch or by a framework error handler, which converts a fail-fast invariant into a logged and ignored one.

Template-literal messages are evaluated eagerly on every successful call; for expensive diagnostics, pass Node's supported message function to an assertion method or compute the detail only on failure.

variants.name: Portable invariant() helper that throws
variants.idiom_name: function invariant(condition, message) { if (!condition) throw new Error(message); }
variants.implementation_notes: Outside Node - browsers, workers, shared libraries - there is no assertion module, so the realization is a two-line helper: a function that throws a plain Error when the condition is false and returns otherwise. It costs nothing but is always active, so it is the right choice for invariants that must hold in production; for one-off checks a bare if (!condition) throw new Error(message) is equivalent without the helper.
pitfalls: A plain Error carries no type: callers cannot distinguish an invariant violation from any other failure unless a dedicated error class is thrown.
Helpers are easy to import into code that should validate instead of assert, which turns expected input errors into crashes.
